title: Influnet
tagline: Find real creators. Run every collab to the finish.
summary: An influencer-marketing platform where brands post campaigns, shortlist creators who have proved they own their accounts, agree terms in writing and pay stage by stage — on the web and in a native mobile app.
description: Creators and brands mostly meet in Instagram DMs and email threads, where replies take hours or days and deals fall through. Influnet replaces that with one link: a creator puts their Influnet profile in their bio, a brand taps it, and a collaboration request lands instantly.

I built it as a Turborepo monorepo — a Next.js 16 web app with its API routes, a separate marketing site, and an Expo / React Native app for iOS and Android — on top of Supabase for auth, Postgres and row-level security.
Every collaboration moves through a 12-stage pipeline with a Kanban workspace, real-time chat on Stream, written terms and Razorpay payment gates, with an admin approval flow on top.

features.title: Verified creator profiles
features.desc: Creators prove they own their social accounts before brands can shortlist them, with live follower, view and engagement stats on a shareable link-in-bio page.

features.title: 12-stage campaign pipeline
features.desc: Every collab moves from request to brief, terms, content, approval and payout on a Kanban workspace both sides can see.

features.title: Chat and notifications
features.desc: Stream-powered chat with persisted history and an in-app notification bell, so requests get answered in minutes instead of days.

features.title: Payment gates
features.desc: Razorpay payments are released stage by stage against agreed deliverables, with written terms attached to every deal.

highlights: Turborepo monorepo: Next.js web app, marketing site and Expo mobile app sharing one backend
Supabase Postgres with row-level security and a documented PII lockdown
End-to-end Playwright suites covering requests, chat, freemium limits and access guards
Phone OTP sign-in through a Supabase edge function
challenge: Creators and brands mostly meet in Instagram DMs and email threads. Replies take hours or days, follower counts are easy to fake, and the terms of a deal live in someone's chat history — so collaborations stall or fall apart halfway.
Brands needed to know who they were actually talking to before they replied. Creators needed one place for every deal, and both sides needed a shared record of what was agreed and what had been paid.

architecture.caption: Three apps in one Turborepo monorepo share a single Supabase backend. Chat and payments run on Stream and Razorpay.

steps.title: Prove it's you
steps.desc: Creators verify they own their social accounts. Unverified profiles show a neutral 'ownership not verified' label, and a business sees a warning before sending a request.

steps.title: Request
steps.desc: A brand finds a creator through search or their link-in-bio profile and sends a collaboration request, which lands as an in-app notification.

steps.title: Agree in writing
steps.desc: Accepting a request opens a project and a Stream chat. Terms, deliverables and budget are discussed and recorded inside the project.

steps.title: Work the pipeline
steps.desc: The project moves through 12 stages — deposit, planning, shooting, editing, review, revisions, approval — with a 'whose turn' owner on each stage.

steps.title: Get paid
steps.desc: Advance and final payments go through Razorpay. Only the signature-verified webhook can mark a payment as paid; the client never self-reports it.

Creator landing page: four questions answered before you reply to a brand.
The same product on the web and in the iOS / Android app.
How a collab moves from request to final payment.
Stage by stage: discussion, deposit, shooting, review, payment.
Under the hood: three apps, one Supabase backend.

decisions.title: Keep the stack, buy at the service level
decisions.desc: No marketplace framework. Next.js and Supabase stay the core, and chat, payments and email are bought as services (Stream, Razorpay, Resend) instead of being rebuilt.

decisions.title: One app, scaled horizontally
decisions.desc: The web app and its API routes deploy as one unit. When background work grows, the plan is to split out a worker — not to split frontend from backend.

decisions.title: The database enforces the rules
decisions.desc: Row-level security decides who can read and write each table, and a documented PII lockdown keeps private fields out of public profiles. A bug in the UI can't leak data on its own.

decisions.title: Payments the client can't fake
decisions.desc: Razorpay orders are created on the server and a signature-verified webhook is the only writer of 'paid'. Stage gates check that record, not anything the browser says.

roadmap: Reviews and ratings on completed projects, written once per side and enforced by row-level security.
A completed-work showcase on each creator's public profile, feeding rating and completed count into discovery.
Per-project progress bars and a 'whose turn' label on both dashboards.

title: Buziness OS
tagline: Run your business from one intelligent operating system
summary: A multi-tenant revenue workspace for Indian sales teams: a pipeline, an evidence-based sourcing agent, a softphone contact centre and a meeting bot that writes the minutes — with plans, metered credits and two admin consoles on top.
description: Small revenue teams run sales across a CRM, a dialler, a meeting notetaker and a lead database, with nothing connecting them. Buziness OS puts the working parts in one workspace per client company, with its own members, plan, modules, credits and data.

The real backends today are the pipeline, the sourcing agent (evidence-based email lookup), the contact centre (TeleCMI softphone with Gemini transcription) and the meeting notetaker (Meeting BaaS bots, minutes written by Gemini). Campaigns, omnichannel, voice agents and workflows are designed screens that only the demo workspace shows.

Underneath is the part that makes it sellable: every API route goes through one guard that resolves the workspace, checks the plan, module and role, rate-limits, and takes credits up front with an automatic refund on failure.

features.title: Pipeline and contacts
features.desc: Leads move across stages on a board or table; contacts are derived from the same record, and the dashboard shows live counts for real workspaces.

features.title: Sourcing agent
features.desc: Finds and verifies a prospect's business email from evidence and shows a readable trace of how it got there — no invented data presented as findings.

features.title: Contact centre
features.desc: A TeleCMI softphone in the browser. Calls are recorded and transcribed with Gemini, charged once however many times transcription is retried.

features.title: Meeting notetaker
features.desc: Dispatches a Meeting BaaS bot to Google Meet, Zoom or Teams, ingests the transcript by webhook and writes minutes with Gemini when the call ends.

features.title: Plans, modules and credits
features.desc: Six plans, per-workspace grants and prices, a platform kill switch, a monthly allowance and a full credit ledger.

features.title: Two admin surfaces
features.desc: /admin for each workspace (members, roles, invites, usage, audit log) and /platform for the team that runs every workspace.

metrics.label: AI and telephony services wired in

challenge: Revenue teams at small Indian companies stitch together a CRM, a dialler, a meeting notetaker and a lead database. Every tool has its own login and its own copy of the customer, and nothing carries over when a lead becomes a call becomes a meeting.

The product also had to be sellable as SaaS from day one: many client companies on one deployment, each paying for different modules, with AI actions that cost real money and have to be metered, limited and refunded fairly.

architecture.caption: One Next.js app on Railway. Every API route goes through the same guard before it reaches Neon Postgres or a paid AI service.

steps.title: Resolve the workspace
steps.desc: The guard blocks cross-site writes, resolves the session and workspace, and checks the workspace is active.

steps.title: Check entitlement
steps.desc: Modules resolve strongest-first: platform kill switch, platform override, the plan's module list, then the workspace admin's own switch.

steps.title: Check the role
steps.desc: Each route declares its access level — public, user, member, write, org admin or super admin — and the guard enforces it.

steps.title: Charge up front
steps.desc: Credits are taken with a single conditional UPDATE … WHERE balance ≥ cost, so balances never go negative and concurrent requests can't overspend.

steps.title: Run, log, refund
steps.desc: The handler runs; usage and outcome are logged. If it fails, the credits come back automatically.

screens.caption: The dashboard in the one-click demo workspace (sample company, sample data).
Leads on one pipeline, from new to won.
The sourcing agent: evidence-based business-email lookup with a visible trace.
The contact centre: a browser softphone with Gemini transcription.
Workspace admin: plan, credits used, members and audit log.

decisions.title: One guard, not per-route checks
decisions.desc: Tenancy, entitlement, roles, rate limits, credits and logging live in a single api() wrapper. A route declares what it needs and never re-implements any of it.

decisions.title: Atomic credits with refunds
decisions.desc: A conditional UPDATE makes overspending impossible under concurrency, failed actions are refunded, and a call's transcription is charged once however often it's retried.

decisions.title: Least-privilege database role
decisions.desc: The app connects as a restricted role; migrations run with a separate privileged URL. A compromised app can't change the schema.

decisions.title: Be honest about what's real
decisions.desc: Modules without a backend show a 'not set up yet' state in real workspaces; only the sample-data demo shows their designed screens.

roadmap: Razorpay top-ups for credits (orders → webhook → ledger) and invoices, replacing manual top-ups.
Email delivery for invites and password resets, plus email verification and TOTP 2FA for platform admins.
Per-workspace telephony settings instead of one shared TeleCMI account.
Real backends for campaigns, omnichannel, voice agents and workflows.

title: Mithra Whole Foods
role: Full-Stack Engineer — storefront, commerce backend & CMS
tagline: Traditional foods, sold through a modern headless store
summary: A complete grocery store for millets, cold-pressed oils, ghee and traditional foods — Next.js storefront on a Medusa v2 commerce backend with cart, checkout, Stripe payments, search, wishlist and a custom homepage CMS.
description: Mithra Whole Foods sells traditional, chemical-free foods and needed to move off an ageing template store onto something that feels premium and converts.

I rebuilt it as a headless store: a Next.js 15 storefront talking to a Medusa v2 backend on PostgreSQL. The full commerce path works end to end — catalogue, optimistic cart, customer accounts, multi-step checkout, Stripe payments, order history, wishlist and an in-house search engine with no external search service.
A custom homepage CMS module with an admin live-preview page lets the client change banners and featured collections without a developer.

features.desc: The cart updates instantly, then reconciles with the backend and rolls back with a clear message if something is out of stock.

features.title: Four-step checkout
features.desc: Address, shipping, payment and review, with Stripe payments and order confirmation.

features.title: In-house search
features.desc: Product search runs inside the Medusa backend — fast, free and no third-party index to keep in sync.

features.title: Homepage CMS
features.desc: A custom Medusa module plus a live-preview admin page for banners, offers and featured products.

highlights: pnpm + Turborepo monorepo with storefront and commerce backend
Stripe payments, customer auth and address book
Production audit, QA report and deployment runbook delivered with the build
Client's own wordmark traced to SVG and real product photography throughout
challenge: Mithra Whole Foods sells chemical-free traditional foods — millets, cold-pressed oils, ghee, jaggery — and it was running on an ageing template store that didn't feel premium, couldn't be extended, and needed a developer for every banner change.
The rebuild had to keep the full commerce path working end to end, stay cheap to run for a small brand, and hand day-to-day content back to the client.

architecture.caption: A Next.js storefront on Vercel talks to a Medusa v2 backend on Railway, which owns the data in Neon Postgres and takes payments through Stripe.

steps.title: Check out

steps.title: Edit the homepage

decisions.title: Headless, on an open-source commerce core
decisions.desc: Medusa v2 provides orders, carts, customers and payments as a backend; the storefront is free to look like the brand instead of a template.

decisions.desc: The cart feels instant, but the backend is the source of truth — a rejected change rolls back visibly instead of silently drifting.

decisions.title: Measure before migrating
decisions.desc: A slow store prompted 'should we move to Supabase?'. Measuring showed ~290 ms per query from the backend–database distance; a same-region link is 1–3 ms. The answer was region, not vendor.

title: Tecstellar Command Center
tagline: One console for every app we ship
summary: A command centre for a portfolio of consumer apps: agents work call queues, supervisors manage access and escalations, and owners see users, revenue, funnels and SLA health across every app on one screen.
description: Tecstellar runs several consumer apps — RealBroks, IronDrobe and more on the way. Users, payments, tickets and follow-ups were spread across separate dashboards, one per app.

TCC pulls them into one console with three role-based views. Agents get a focused 3-step call panel driven entirely by keyboard shortcuts; supervisors manage team access, language and state allocation and an escalations inbox; owners get an all-apps dashboard with funnel, leaderboard, churn and an India map built with D3.
Operational data syncs live across browsers through Firestore, and calls are placed through TeleCMI with explicit safety modes before production dialling is switched on.

features.title: Keyboard-first agent workspace
features.desc: 1–5 for status, Q–I for outcome, Enter to save, S to skip, T to raise a ticket — agents never reach for the mouse.

features.title: Queue-based access
features.desc: Supervisors tick which queues each agent can see, with live coverage gaps and reachable-user counts per language and state.

features.title: Owner dashboard
features.desc: Users, MRR, dues, funnel, agent leaderboard, churn and SLA health across every app.

features.title: Geography view
features.desc: A D3 map of India with state boundaries and circles sized by user count.

highlights: Runs on Firestore or fully offline on localStorage — chosen automatically
Customer data layer split from TCC-owned data so the real app databases can be swapped in later
Mid-call reroute and escalation wired to a live supervisor queue
TeleCMI calling with documented dialling safety modes
challenge: Tecstellar runs several consumer apps — RealBroks and IronDrobe live, Influnet and Vehigo on the way. Users, payments, tickets and follow-ups lived in separate dashboards, one per app, and the calling team worked from spreadsheets.
They needed one console where agents call the right customers, supervisors see who's falling behind and owners see the whole portfolio — without waiting for every app's database to be wired in first.

title: Casa Harmony
tagline: Enterprise accounting for homeowner associations
summary: A secure multi-tenant service desk and ERP for homeowner associations, modelled on Oracle E-Business Suite — configurable chart of accounts, double-entry general ledger, and database-enforced tenant isolation.
description: Homeowner associations need real accounting — dues, receivables, general ledger — plus a service desk, without one association ever seeing another’s data.

Casa Harmony enforces isolation at the database: every tenant table carries a tenant_id and PostgreSQL row-level security. The chart of accounts follows Oracle’s Key Flexfield model with configurable segments, value sets and cross-validation rules.

An Accounts Receivable subledger posts balanced double-entry journals to the GL — the pattern future AP, cash and fixed-asset subledgers follow. Security scaffolding covers TOTP MFA, field-level encryption, immutable audit logs, card tokenisation and CCPA data-subject flows.

features.title: Row-level security
features.desc: Tenant isolation enforced by PostgreSQL itself, not just application code.

features.title: Oracle-style chart of accounts
features.desc: Key Flexfield segments (6 by default, up to 15), qualifiers, value sets and validated code combinations.

features.title: Double-entry subledgers
features.desc: Accounts Receivable posts balanced journals to the general ledger.

features.title: Compliance scaffolding
features.desc: TOTP MFA, field-level encryption at rest, audit logging, card tokenisation and CCPA flows.

highlights: FastAPI + SQLAlchemy 2 + Alembic migrations on PostgreSQL 16
Superadmin and per-association sysadmin roles
Compliance control map and TLS guidance documented with the code
Docker Compose locally, Render blueprint for deployment
challenge: Homeowner associations collect dues, pay vendors and hold reserve funds that must stay separate by law — but most run on spreadsheets and small-business accounting tools that don't understand funds, approvals or a service desk.
A property-management firm serving several associations needed one system for all of them, where staff can work across communities and no association can ever see another's books.

architecture.caption: A Next.js front end over a FastAPI backend. Every request binds its tenant into Postgres, where row-level security decides what rows exist.

steps.title: Bind the tenant
steps.desc: Each transaction runs SELECT set_config('app.current_tenant', …, true) — a SET LOCAL — so every query is filtered by RLS policies, not by remembering a WHERE clause.

steps.title: Raise and route work
steps.desc: Residents report issues on the service desk; tickets carry priority, owner and SLA, and turn into purchase orders when a vendor is needed.

steps.title: Procure to pay
steps.desc: PO lines carry flexfield distributions; multi-level approval by amount; AP invoices are 2-way matched (invoice ≤ PO) before approval.

steps.title: Create accounting
steps.desc: Subledger Accounting drafts GL journal batches — debit expense, credit AP — grouped per fund, so each fund's journal nets to zero.

steps.title: Post and report
steps.desc: A GL accountant approves control totals and posts; balances land by period, code combination and fund, and the trial balance exports by fund.

screens.caption: The HOA admin dashboard in the demo (fictional association and residents).
The service desk: tickets by category and status.
Payables: invoices matched against purchase orders before payment.
Journal entry with an Oracle-style code combination — balanced.
The board dashboard: operating and reserve funds, kept separate.
Under the hood: Next.js, FastAPI, row-level security, Postgres.

decisions.title: Isolation in the database
decisions.desc: tenant_id plus Postgres row-level security on every tenant table. A missed filter in application code returns nothing instead of another association's data.

decisions.title: Borrow Oracle's model, not its weight
decisions.desc: Key Flexfield chart of accounts, GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS and subledger accounting follow Oracle EBS table design, so accountants recognise it and future AP, cash and fixed-asset modules follow one pattern.

decisions.title: Funds can't be skipped
decisions.desc: Distribution resolution rejects any account combination without a Fund value, which makes fund accounting a guarantee rather than a convention.

decisions.title: One front end, two data modes
decisions.desc: The same 45 screens run on an in-browser demo store or the live API, so the client could review the product before the backend shipped.

roadmap: Cash management and fixed-asset subledgers on the same Subledger Accounting pattern.
Go-live checklist: data migration from the client's current books and a deploy runbook on Render / Railway.
Field-level encryption and CCPA access / portability / erasure flows, moved from scaffolding to production use.
Scheduled assessments and dunning runs on the job scheduler.

title: WassupOS
role: Full-Stack Engineer — platform, auth & voice agent
tagline: A WhatsApp CRM with an AI on the front line
summary: A multi-tenant WhatsApp CRM: each company gets an inbox, scored leads, broadcasts, campaigns and orders, an AI sales assistant that answers on WhatsApp strictly from the company's own knowledge base, and a Python voice agent for WhatsApp calls.
description: Businesses in India sell on WhatsApp, but their leads and follow-ups live somewhere else. WassupOS brings the CRM into WhatsApp: a live inbox, leads scored hot, warm or scrap, broadcasts and templates, campaigns and orders — one workspace per company.

Incoming messages are answered by an AI sales assistant through the WhatsApp Cloud API. It answers only from the company's knowledge base, built from its website and PDFs, and says it will check with the team when the knowledge base doesn't cover a question.

A platform admin onboards companies, switches modules on per tenant (enforced on every API route), and stores integration credentials in an AES-256-GCM vault. A separate Python voice agent answers WhatsApp calls, costed per call before scaling.

features.title: Grounded AI replies
features.desc: The assistant's only source of truth is the tenant's knowledge base — no invented prices, products or industries.

features.title: Knowledge from websites and PDFs
features.desc: Websites are fetched and stripped; PDFs are read from their text layer, with a model only for image-only scans.

features.title: Company workspace
features.desc: Inbox, leads with temperature, contacts, broadcasts, templates, campaigns and orders, with realtime updates.

features.title: Per-tenant modules
features.desc: The platform admin enables modules per company; backend guards enforce them on every route.

features.title: Voice agent
features.desc: A Pipecat pipeline answers WhatsApp calls over WebRTC, in English and Tamil.

challenge: Indian small businesses sell on WhatsApp, but their leads, broadcasts and follow-ups live in notebooks or a CRM nobody opens, and messages that arrive after hours go unanswered.
The client wanted a SaaS they could sell to many companies: one deployment, each company getting only the modules it pays for, with an AI that answers customers without ever making things up.

architecture.caption: The Next.js app is the multi-tenant core. The voice agent is a separate Python service that WhatsApp calls reach directly over WebRTC.

steps.title: Onboard a company
steps.desc: The platform admin creates a tenant, enables modules and adds integration credentials to an encrypted vault.

steps.title: Build its knowledge
steps.desc: The company's website and PDFs become knowledge chunks — text layers read directly, a model only for image-only scans.

steps.title: Answer on WhatsApp
steps.desc: A Cloud API webhook loads the tenant's knowledge and the conversation, and the AI replies under a knowledge-base-only rule.

steps.title: Work the lead
steps.desc: Conversations land in a live inbox; leads are scored HOT, WARM or SCRAP and can sync to Google Sheets.

steps.title: Pick up the call
steps.desc: WhatsApp calls go to a separate Python voice agent: speech-to-text, LLM and text-to-speech over a direct WebRTC session.

screens.caption: The AI assistant answering from the knowledge base — and checking with the team when it can't (example conversation).
The company workspace's modules.
The voice agent's preflight checks.
What a voice call actually costs, by stage.

decisions.title: The knowledge base is the only truth
decisions.desc: Without it, the model told a paying-guest rooms business's customer it was a scrap trading company. The prompt now forbids any fact the knowledge base doesn't contain.

decisions.title: Don't use a model where a parser will do
decisions.desc: PDF ingestion went through an LLM and timed out (504) on 23-page uploads. Reading the embedded text layer is instant, free and complete; the model is only for scans.

decisions.title: Guards on the server, not the menu
decisions.desc: Module switches are checked in every API route; the UI hides disabled features, but the backend is what refuses them.

decisions.title: Cost it before you scale it
decisions.desc: A per-stage voice cost model showed TTS is 86% of an English call and Tamil doubles LLM tokens — so reply length is a cost lever.

roadmap: Connect the voice agent's call outcomes to the CRM's leads.
Resolve the billing question that decides whether Tamil calls cost 1.2× or 1.6× English.

title: Amretri Healthcare
tagline: An in-browser lead assistant and a Google Sheets backend — no servers to run
summary: A 14-page website for a hospital pharmacy operator, with AMRI — a chat assistant that qualifies leads entirely in the visitor's browser — and a backend made of one Google Sheet and one Apps Script instead of a server and database.
description: Amretri Healthcare runs hospital pharmacies, supplies pharmacists and buys medicines in bulk for hospitals across India, and has done since 2009. Their buyers are hospital owners and administrators, and the sales team needs a few hard facts — hospital, city, beds, monthly pharmacy sales — before a call is worth making.

I designed and built the whole thing: a 14-page TanStack Start site (home, about, six service pages, pharmacist registration, blog, contact and legal pages), AMRI, the chat assistant on the homepage, and a backend that is nothing more than a Google Sheet and one Apps Script web app.

The constraint shaped every decision: a services company with no engineers on staff. Whatever I shipped had to cost close to nothing to run, and the team had to be able to work it from tools they already use — Google Sheets and WhatsApp.

features.title: AMRI chat assistant
features.desc: Identifies the visitor, answers from a 52-question knowledge base and runs six guided lead flows — all client-side, with no model or API call per message.

features.title: Google Sheets as the CRM
features.desc: The chat's welcome step and every site form land as rows: one tab per form type, created on first use, with new columns added automatically.

features.title: A blog with no CMS
features.desc: Posts are rows (title, category, date, read time, author, HTML body). The blog fetches them at runtime, so publishing needs no redeploy; three built-in posts render if the sheet is unreachable.

features.title: WhatsApp hand-off
features.desc: Finished intakes become a pre-filled wa.me message, and a WhatsApp button floats right above the chat launcher.

features.title: Safety-aware answers
features.desc: Answers about licences and medico-legal topics automatically carry a note that final regulatory decisions need a qualified professional.

features.title: SEO groundwork
features.desc: Per-page titles and descriptions, canonical URLs, a sitemap, and schema.org MedicalBusiness and FAQPage data on the homepage.

metrics.label: App servers or databases to run
Apps Script behind every form and the blog

challenge: Hospital buyers don't fill in long forms. They ask specific questions — “can you take over my pharmacy?”, “I need two night-shift pharmacists” — and expect an answer straight away.
The usual fix is a hosted chatbot, a backend, a database and an LLM bill. For a team with nobody to maintain it, that is a monthly cost and a system that slowly breaks.
So the brief became: answer the common questions instantly, turn intent into a qualified lead, and put every lead where the team already works — without anything to host.

architecture.alt: AMRI system architecture: the website and chat widget run in the visitor's browser, post JSON to a Google Apps Script web app that writes to a Google Sheet, and hand completed briefs to WhatsApp.
architecture.caption: Everything left of the Apps Script runs in the visitor's browser. The dashed box is the next phase.

steps.title: Identify
steps.desc: Before the first message AMRI asks for a name and email. The visitor is remembered in localStorage, and the contact is posted to the sheet as an Inquiries row.

steps.title: Route
steps.desc: Every message hits intent rules first. Phrases about takeovers, staffing, purchase rates, setups, licences or a callback start the matching lead flow.

steps.title: Answer
steps.desc: Everything else is token-matched against 52 reviewed Q&As in 11 service sections, with a confidence threshold. Below it, AMRI offers the menu or a human instead of guessing.

steps.title: Qualify
steps.desc: Each flow asks 3–7 questions one at a time and validates the answer — contacts need 8+ digits or an @, and a bare “yes” is rejected. FAQ questions mid-flow are answered without losing the place.

steps.title: Hand off
steps.desc: The completed brief becomes a pre-filled WhatsApp message to the Amretri team — one tap from the visitor.

screens.caption: AMRI end to end: identify the visitor → answer a free-text question → run the pharmacy-takeover intake → hand the brief to WhatsApp.
Homepage, with AMRI's launcher bottom-right.
Six service lines, each with its own page and enquiry form.
Service page for hospital pharmacy acquisition and management.
Its proposal form posts straight to the sheet.
Every form → one Apps Script → a tab per form type.
The blog reads the Blogs tab as JSON: a row is a post.

decisions.title: Rules before models
decisions.desc: Buyers ask a narrow set of questions whose answers carry commercial and compliance weight. A rule engine gives the same reviewed answer every time, instantly and for free — and it's the right first layer even once a model is added.

decisions.title: A spreadsheet instead of a server
decisions.desc: One Apps Script replaces the API and the database. doPost routes each form to its own tab and grows columns for new fields, so adding a form needs no backend change. doGet serves the blog.

decisions.title: Meet the team where it works
decisions.desc: Leads arrive as sheet rows and WhatsApp messages, not in a dashboard nobody opens. There was nothing new for the team to learn.

decisions.title: Trade-offs, stated plainly
decisions.desc: Apps Script redirects break CORS for JSON posts, so forms send with mode: 'no-cors' and confirm optimistically. The web-app URL is public by design, so spam filtering in the script is the next hardening step.

roadmap: An on-device small language model (WebLLM on WebGPU) to phrase answers and handle questions the rules miss — weights cached in the browser, still no server or API key.
Semantic search over the knowledge base with in-browser embeddings, replacing token overlap.
Log completed intake briefs to the sheet as well as WhatsApp, so every qualified lead is on record.
Spam protection on the Apps Script endpoint (honeypot field and rate limiting).

title: JaiSathya Inc.
role: Lead Full-Stack Architect & Visual CMS Engineer
tagline: One site for eight businesses — edited in place by the owner
summary: The corporate site for JaiSathya Inc., a holding company with eight businesses — restaurants, catering, food distribution, real estate, marketing, DataEQ, Ayuryum and a cricket club — with a visual CMS that lets the owner edit the live page layout directly.
description: JaiSathya Inc. is a founder-led holding company with eight businesses across hospitality, food, real estate, technology and sport, including three restaurant brands — Manam, Kaanchi and Malgudi Cafe.
I built the site on TanStack Start with a visual CMS from scratch: the owner edits text and images on the real page layout instead of filling in disconnected forms, and publishes when ready.
Every editable thing is one row in a single documents table with draft and published JSON, and the editor infers its form from the document's shape — so adding a field never needs a migration.

features.title: In-place visual editing
features.desc: Editable regions on the actual page layout; click text or an image and change it where it lives.

features.title: Draft, then publish
features.desc: Saves go to draft_data; visitors see published_data, and publish copies one into the other in a single write.

features.title: Media library
features.desc: Cloudinary-backed, with the public_id as the row key and alt text stored once per image, so fixing it fixes every use.

features.title: Shared documents
features.desc: A brand's summary card is one document shown on both the homepage and its own page.

challenge: JaiSathya runs eight very different businesses, from restaurants to a professional cricket club, and needed one site that presents them as a group while giving each restaurant brand its own page.
Content changes constantly — menus, events, holdings — and the owner didn't want a developer in the loop, or a generic CMS whose forms look nothing like the page they're editing.

architecture.caption: TanStack Start serves both the public site and the visual admin. Server functions read and write one documents table and the Cloudinary media library.

steps.title: Model pages as documents
steps.desc: A registry maps each page to its sections and each section to a (collection, slug) document — the only structure the admin needs.

steps.title: Edit in place
steps.desc: The visual editor wraps the real components in Editable regions; the generic ObjectEditor builds a form from whatever JSON the document holds.

steps.title: Pick media
steps.desc: Images come from a Cloudinary-backed library; alt text lives on the media row, not on each page that uses it.

steps.title: Save a draft
steps.desc: Every admin write targets draft_data, so nothing a visitor sees changes until it's published.

steps.title: Publish
steps.desc: publishDocuments copies draft_data into published_data — the only write path that touches what visitors see.

screens.caption: jaisathya.com — the group homepage.
The homepage's ecosystem of eight holdings.
Manam's brand page.
How an edit flows: click, pick media, save draft, publish.
DataEQ's holding page.
Under the hood: registry, documents table, Cloudinary.

decisions.title: One table instead of a table per type
decisions.desc: Holdings, brands, home sections and cards are all documents with JSON data. The registry supplies structure, so new content types need no schema change.

decisions.title: Draft and published side by side
decisions.desc: Two columns on the same row make publish a single SET, and preview simply reads the other column.

decisions.title: The form comes from the data
decisions.desc: ObjectEditor infers fields from the document's shape, so a new field in the content is editable immediately.

decisions.title: Cloudinary ids as keys
decisions.desc: The media row's primary key is the Cloudinary public_id — never two identifiers for the same asset.

roadmap: Side-by-side preview of draft vs published before publishing.
Per-document revision history.
Role-based access for brand managers who should only edit their own brand.
Event and menu content types for the restaurants.

title: Email Finder
tagline: Finds a work email — and tells you how much to trust it
summary: Give it a name and a company website; it gathers evidence across seven tiers — free ones first — infers the domain’s email pattern, and only reports an address as certain as the evidence allows.
description: Most email finders guess a pattern and hope. This engine gathers evidence and weighs it: DNS and MX records, a relevance-scored site crawl, sitemaps, GitHub commit authors, linked PDFs like staff directories, and the Internet Archive for blocked sites.
Paid tiers — search queries, a browser transport for JavaScript-heavy or firewalled pages, and mail-server verification — only run when the free tiers cannot settle the question.
Results keep three claims separate on purpose: published, inferred and verified, because each one fails in a different way. It runs as a web app plus a background worker on Railway.

features.title: Seven evidence tiers
features.desc: Free sources first; paid search, browser and verification only when needed — costs stay predictable.

features.title: Pattern inference
features.desc: Learns the domain’s email format from any name/address pairs it finds, then ranks a candidate ladder.

features.title: Honest confidence
features.desc: Published, inferred and verified are reported separately — never more certain than the evidence.

features.title: Catch-all detection
features.desc: Detects domains that accept every address before trusting a mail-server “yes”.

highlights: Web app and worker deployed as separate Railway services
Worker waits for the database instead of crashing on cold starts
Drizzle migrations with separate local and production configs
Unit-tested inference with Vitest
challenge: Sales teams need a person's work email, and most tools answer by guessing a pattern (first.last@) and labelling it 'verified'. On catch-all domains that label is meaningless, and every bounce hurts the sender's reputation.
The goal was a finder that spends as little as possible per lookup and is honest about certainty — including saying 'don't mail this person here' when the evidence says so.

architecture.caption: A Next.js web app enqueues lookups; a separate worker runs the tiered engine and writes results to Postgres under forced row-level security.

steps.title: Resolve the domain
steps.desc: DNS and MX first — free, and enough to rule out domains that can't receive mail at all.

steps.title: Gather free evidence
steps.desc: A relevance-scored crawl, sitemaps, GitHub commit authors, linked PDFs like staff directories, and the Internet Archive for sites that block crawlers.

steps.title: Infer the pattern
steps.desc: Name/address pairs found along the way teach the domain's format; the engine ranks a candidate ladder from it.

steps.title: Spend only if needed
steps.desc: Search, a browser transport for WAF-blocked or JS-rendered pages, and verification run only when the free tiers can't settle it.

steps.title: Verify honestly
steps.desc: Catch-all detection runs before the ladder; a verified rejection of every candidate returns fail — a useful 'don't mail' rather than a guess.

screens.caption: A lookup working through the evidence tiers (example person and domain).
The confidence tiers a result can earn.
Under the hood: web, queue, worker and Postgres with forced RLS.

decisions.title: Three claims, never merged
decisions.desc: Published, deliverable and predicted fail differently, so they're reported separately. Only published and deliverable together earns 'confirmed'.

decisions.title: Cheapest evidence first
decisions.desc: Four free tiers run before any paid search, browser or verification call, keeping per-lookup cost predictable.

decisions.title: Don't trust the ORM's RLS
decisions.desc: Querying pg_policies showed drizzle-kit pushing policies with no USING clause — RLS on, but every row visible. The real predicates live in rls-force.sql, re-run after every push.

decisions.title: A worker that waits
decisions.desc: Web and worker deploy as separate Railway services; the worker waits for the database on cold starts instead of crash-looping.

roadmap: Wire in a production verification provider so more results can reach 'confirmed'.
Self-hosted browser transport to keep tier 5 costs flat.
Per-lookup cost reporting in the dashboard.

title: Reframe
tagline: Read anything, beautifully — without a word rewritten
summary: Paste an article, PDF or link and get back a lossless, visual reading experience — headings, callouts, definitions and comparisons made explicit — while every word stays the author’s own.
description: AI summaries lose the author's voice and quietly drop detail. Reframe takes the opposite promise: it never rewrites your material, it re-architects it into callouts, definitions, comparisons and steps.

The source is parsed and split into deterministically addressed units before any model runs. The model — Groq's llama-3.3-70b behind a rotating key pool — only returns block types and unit ids; the server rehydrates every word from the original.
Without an API key it runs in a clearly flagged demo mode on deterministic heuristics, so it always works and costs nothing to try. Analytics and feedback flow to a Google Sheet through Apps Script.

features.title: Lossless by construction
features.desc: The model has no channel to emit body text — it returns addresses — so paraphrase is structurally impossible rather than merely checked.

features.title: Coverage guarantee
features.desc: Every source unit must be referenced exactly once. Missing or duplicated content throws and the section falls back to plain text.

features.title: Quoted fragments
features.desc: Any number or date the model highlights must be a literal substring of its unit, or the block is demoted to prose.

features.title: Demo mode
features.desc: Works with no key and no cost, clearly labelled in the interface.

challenge: People read long material — papers, docs, articles — and AI summaries are the usual shortcut. But a summary paraphrases, drops detail, and can confidently state things the author never wrote.
Reframe set out to make long text easier to read without changing a single word of it: find the structure that was always implicit and make it visible.

architecture.caption: The browser holds the library; /api/transform parses, addresses and verifies; the model only ever sees numbered units and returns ids.

steps.title: Parse
steps.desc: Markup is structure, not content — headings, lists and tables are parsed directly rather than classified by a model.

steps.title: Address
steps.desc: Text is split into deterministically addressed units like p0 and l1_0.

steps.title: Classify
steps.desc: The model receives numbered units and returns block types, unit ids and short scaffolding words — about 15 output tokens per block.

steps.title: Verify
steps.desc: assertCoverage checks every unit is used exactly once; any highlighted value must be a quoted fragment of its unit.

steps.title: Rehydrate
steps.desc: The server rebuilds every body field from the source text, and the reader renders the blocks.

screens.caption: Reframe's paste-in screen (running locally in demo mode).
Source text re-architected into a callout, a definition and a comparison.
What the model actually returns: block types and unit ids, never text.
Under the hood: parse, address, classify, verify.

decisions.title: Addresses, not text
decisions.desc: Once the model can only return ids, verbatim stops being something to check and becomes a property of the architecture — and output cost drops sharply.

decisions.title: A verifier that can't fail isn't one
decisions.desc: An early fidelity check reported 100% verbatim while the model rewrote sentences in an unchecked field. Every guarantee now has a test that fails before its fix.

decisions.title: Plain-but-complete beats polished-but-lossy
decisions.desc: Any coverage or fragment violation demotes the block to prose instead of dropping or inventing content.

decisions.title: Write the divergence down
decisions.desc: An ADR described a pipeline that no longer existed. Recording what actually runs — and when it changed — is now part of the process.

roadmap: PDF and link ingestion polish for the students-first wedge.
Cross-device sync once the validation metric gates pass (v0 is localStorage-only).
Replace Sheets analytics with a real store after the gates pass.

title: Black Hole
tagline: Throw in. Pull out. Anywhere.
summary: A private clipboard between your Mac and your phone. Copy on the Mac and it is on your phone a second later — over your own Wi-Fi, with no account, no relay server, and everything expiring on both devices.
description: Moving a link or a screenshot from laptop to phone usually means messaging yourself. Black Hole makes it automatic: copy on the Mac and it appears on the phone, no app to open first.
Devices pair once with a 6-digit code and a QR scan, then talk directly over the local network — nothing passes through a server and no third party ever sees what you copy.
Items expire after 30 minutes on both devices at once unless pinned. Text, links and images all move the same way, with notifications on both ends.

features.title: No middleman
features.desc: Direct device-to-device transfer on your own Wi-Fi. No account, no cloud.

features.title: Expires everywhere
features.desc: A 30-minute default expiry that clears both devices at once; pin what you want to keep.

features.title: Images too
features.desc: Screenshots and photos move like text, with thumbnails on the shelf.

features.title: One-time pairing
features.desc: A 6-digit code and QR code on the Mac, one scan on the phone.

highlights: Shared Rust core with CLI, desktop and mobile front ends
Respects Android’s background-clipboard limits with a one-tap send
Desktop app at v0.1.2
MIT licensed
challenge: Moving a link or screenshot from laptop to phone usually means messaging yourself or using a cloud clipboard that stores everything you copy on someone else's server.

The goal was the opposite: device to device on your own network, nothing stored anywhere else, and nothing kept longer than you need it — on macOS and Android, despite Android's limits on background clipboard access.

architecture.caption: A Rust core shared by the desktop app and CLI; the Android app speaks the same wire protocol, verified against the Rust implementation.

steps.title: Create identities
steps.desc: Each device generates an Ed25519 key pair; its device id is derived from a BLAKE3 hash of the public key.

steps.title: Pair once
steps.desc: The Mac shows a 6-digit code and a QR; the phone joins with it and both remember each other as paired peers.

steps.title: Discover
steps.desc: Paired devices find each other on the local network with mDNS — no relay or rendezvous server.

steps.title: Teleport
steps.desc: Objects (text, link, image) travel as length-prefixed JSON frames over TCP with BLAKE3 checksums; the receiver files them on its shelf.

steps.title: Expire
steps.desc: Every object carries an expiry (30 minutes by default); the TTL reaper clears it on both devices unless it's pinned.

screens.caption: Real output: pairing two devices with a 6-digit code.
Real output: a link delivered, listed, then reaped when it expires.
Under the hood: one Rust core, thin shells.

decisions.title: No server until it's unavoidable
decisions.desc: Direct device-to-device transfer on the local network; any future relay is planned to only ever see opaque bytes.

decisions.title: One core, thin shells
decisions.desc: Object model, store, identity, discovery and expiry live once in Rust; the Tauri app and CLI are thin layers over it.

decisions.title: Prove the port, don't trust it
decisions.desc: The TypeScript protocol on Android was verified against the real Rust CLI — a real pairing handshake and a real received object over actual TCP — before it was used.

decisions.title: Respect the platform
decisions.desc: Android blocks background clipboard reads, so sending from the phone is one deliberate tap instead of a hack that breaks on the next OS update.

roadmap: iOS app on the same protocol.
QUIC transport and an optional relay for when devices aren't on the same network.
Files beyond text, links and images, with chunked resumable transfer.

title: Streak Doctor
tagline: Your GitHub day, live in the terminal — and next, why it didn't count
summary: An open-source GitHub accountability CLI built around one question streak counters ignore: why didn't that contribution count? Today it reports your live count with a countdown to the end of GitHub's UTC day, lists contributions by repo and draws your year as a heatmap in the terminal; the diagnosis engine is next.
description: Streak tracking is a crowded category. Diagnosis isn't. GitHub silently drops contributions for many reasons — wrong commit email, a fork, a non-default branch, a UTC boundary — and nothing tells you which.

Phase 1 shipped a real CLI on npm that works against the live GitHub API for anyone: today's count and countdown, contributions by repo, and since v0.4.0 a heatmap of the last year drawn in the terminal.

The counting rules are documented in the repo's knowledge base, and a diagnosis engine for the first three causes is the next piece of work, gated on real usage: ship, reach ~200 users, and measure who contributes after an at-risk warning.

features.title: Live today count
features.desc: How many contributions have counted and how long is left before GitHub's UTC day ends, in your own time zone.

features.title: Terminal heatmap
features.desc: streak-doctor heatmap draws the last year's contribution grid in characters.

features.title: Zero install
features.desc: npx streak-doctor <username> works for anyone; it reuses the gh CLI token if you're logged in.

features.title: Core + CLI packages
features.desc: Logic lives in a separate core package with no I/O, ready for other front ends.

challenge: GitHub silently drops contributions for half a dozen reasons — an unlinked commit email, a fork, a non-default branch, a UTC day boundary — and the only symptom is a grey square. Streak trackers count; none of them explain.
The tool had to be zero-friction: run it once with npx, no install, no sign-up, against the live API.

architecture.caption: The CLI is a thin layer of adapters over a pure core package that knows GitHub's contribution rules and UTC day maths.

steps.title: Resolve the user
steps.desc: A username argument, or STREAK_DOCTOR_USER; the token comes from gh auth token or GITHUB_TOKEN.

steps.title: Fetch live activity
steps.desc: Adapters call the GitHub API for the user's recent contributions and events.

steps.title: Apply the rules (next)
steps.desc: The diagnosis engine will check each event against GitHub's documented rules — linked email, default branch, fork, ownership. The rules are written; the engine is next.

steps.title: Mind the day
steps.desc: GitHub's day is UTC; the countdown and 'today' are computed for the user's own time zone.

steps.title: Report
steps.desc: Human output by default, --json with a versioned schema, and exit codes for scripts.

screens.caption: The six reasons a commit doesn't count — the rules the diagnosis engine is being built on.
Real output: today's count and the time left in GitHub's day.
Real output: a year of contributions drawn in the terminal.
Under the hood: a pure core package and a thin CLI.

decisions.title: A wedge, not a feature list
decisions.desc: Streak counting is a crowded category; explaining why a contribution didn't count isn't. Everything in v1 serves that one question.

decisions.title: Core without I/O
decisions.desc: Diagnosis lives in streak-doctor-core with no network or filesystem access, so it's easy to test and ready for other front ends.

decisions.title: Write the platform's rules down
decisions.desc: GitHub's non-obvious counting and timezone rules live in a knowledge base, so fixes don't depend on someone remembering them.

decisions.title: Zero friction
decisions.desc: Published to npm and runnable with npx; it reuses the gh CLI's token when you're already logged in.

roadmap: Diagnosis engine v0 for the first three causes: unlinked email, non-default branch, fork.
A real auth story for the CLI (device flow or PAT) instead of borrowing gh's token.
Streak arithmetic, then watch / daemon notifications that warn before the day ends.
Phase gate: ~200 users; continue if 30%+ contribute after an at-risk warning, stop below 10%.

title: Slate
role: Creator — product, AI pipeline & mobile web
tagline: Say what you did. It files itself.
summary: Hold one button and talk. Slate transcribes the ramble, splits it into separate activities, works out which day each belongs to, closes todos you already wrote down and pulls out what you spent — all in the background.
description: Logging your day is tedious, so nobody does it. Slate turns it into one gesture: hold, talk for as long as you like, let go.

Transcription runs on Whisper large-v3-turbo and reasoning on an open 120B model, both on Groq’s free tier, with a rotating key pool and a live usage monitor. You are only asked a question when getting it wrong would corrupt the log.
It ships today as a web app that looks and behaves like the Android app, so it works on a phone over the local network, with a native Expo app in progress.

features.title: One-button capture
features.desc: Hold to talk, release to file — no forms, no categories to pick.

features.title: Ramble splitting
features.desc: One recording becomes separate activities, each placed on the right day.

features.title: Todo closing
features.desc: Matches what you did against todos you already wrote down and ticks them off.

features.title: Spend extraction
features.desc: Pulls amounts you mention into a spending log automatically.

highlights: Self-signed HTTPS dev server so the phone microphone works over LAN
Groq key-pool rotation with live usage tracking
Research notes on Android capture surfaces and the path to native
Monetisation and strategy documented alongside the code
challenge: Logging what you did is useful and tedious, so nobody keeps it up. Every tracker wants a form, a category and a date for each entry.

The bet: if logging were one gesture — hold, talk, let go — people would do it. That means turning an unstructured ramble into clean, correctly dated entries, cheaply enough to run on free model tiers.

architecture.caption: A capture goes to the cheapest tier that can handle it correctly; validation, dates and the confidence gate always run in code.

steps.title: Capture
steps.desc: Hold to talk. The phone uses Web Speech or sends audio to Whisper; the dev server issues its own certificate so the mic works over the LAN.

steps.title: Guard
steps.desc: Whisper invents text on silence — repetition loops or an echoed prompt — so decoder statistics and a prompt-echo check drop it before it becomes 'activity'.

steps.title: Cache first
steps.desc: Clauses are normalised (fillers stripped, tense kept) and matched against learned patterns with {n} slots; fully known captures cost 0 tokens.

steps.title: One structured call
steps.desc: Only unknown clauses go to gpt-oss-120b in a single call with low reasoning effort.

steps.title: Validate and file
steps.desc: Dedup, date resolution, todo closing and the confidence gate run in code; a question is asked only when a wrong guess would corrupt the log.

screens.caption: One ramble split into an activity, a spend and a closed todo.
Measured: an agent loop vs one structured call vs a cached repeat.
Under the hood: capture, guard, cache, one call.

decisions.title: One call beats an agent loop
decisions.desc: On the same 95-word capture, a 14-call tool loop spent 49,054 tokens in ~17 s and missed an activity; one structured call covered all 12 in ~1 s for ~1,000 tokens. Bounded extraction has nothing to explore.

decisions.title: The cache is the moat
decisions.desc: Every resolved clause is learned, keyed by a signature with numbers as slots — so repeats are free and the cache becomes personal, which competitors can't copy.

decisions.title: Conservative caching
decisions.desc: A wrong cached entry is silent and repeats, so todos, dated clauses, low-confidence items and clauses that lean on a neighbour are never cached.

decisions.title: Nothing logged that wasn't said
decisions.desc: Logging a Whisper hallucination is worse than logging nothing, so transcripts are gated on the decoder's own statistics before anything is filed.

roadmap: Test Whisper properly on the user's own accent and vocabulary — the one risk that gates the native build.
Ship as a PWA and measure whether people keep talking to it after week three.
Capture surfaces on Android: the notification bar is shipped; a Quick Settings tile and home-screen widget are written and waiting on a build.
On-device whisper.cpp for privacy.

title: Ardor
tagline: The companion that follows up until you actually do the thing
summary: An accountability app with a companion character, Ardy, that checks in, follows up and grows with you — built on a pure TypeScript engine with more than a thousand tests, plus a marketing site and waitlist.
description: To-do apps remember what you planned; they don’t care whether you did it. Ardor is built around follow-through: Ardy checks in, nudges and celebrates until the task is actually done.
The scheduling and follow-up engine is pure TypeScript with no platform imports, covered by over 1,000 tests, so the same logic can serve Android, iOS, web and desktop.
A Next.js pre-launch site runs the waitlist, and a product “brain” documents vision, timeline, architecture, retention and metric gates for every phase.

features.title: Follow-through engine
features.desc: Check-ins and follow-ups that adapt until the task is done, not just reminded.

features.title: Ardy the companion
features.desc: A character with moods and growth levels that reacts to your progress.

features.title: Tested core
features.desc: Pure TypeScript engine with 1,000+ tests and no side effects.

features.title: Waitlist site
features.desc: Next.js and Supabase pre-launch site with a waitlist.

highlights: Expo / React Native app in strict TypeScript
Notification bridge isolated behind its own service layer
Architecture decision records for every major choice
Marketing, retention and metrics playbooks in the product brain
challenge: To-do apps remember what you planned and leave the follow-through to you. Reminders get swiped away, lists only grow, and the people who most need accountability are the ones who avoid the app.
Ardor is built around follow-through instead: a companion that reads how you're doing, adapts when and how it nudges, and escalates only when it matters.

architecture.caption: The Expo app renders and reports events; a pure TypeScript engine decides what to nudge, when and how.

steps.title: Detect the state
steps.desc: Six emotional states — intention, drift, active avoidance, overwhelm, guilt spiral, flow — evaluated with deterministic rules, first match wins.

steps.title: Rank the work
steps.desc: A priority queue scores urgency with hyperbolic discounting and the procrastination equation, weighted by deadline and how often a task was ignored.

steps.title: Time the nudge
steps.desc: SM-2 spaced repetition adapted for procrastination, with state multipliers, quiet hours and peak hours.

steps.title: Vary the message
steps.desc: The novelty engine rotates tone, channel, template and sound so nudges don't habituate; two ignores escalate to a full-screen alarm.

steps.title: Learn from the outcome
steps.desc: A feedback loop adjusts the ease factor — up for fast completions, down for snoozes and ignores — and a verifier discounts suspicious completions.

screens.caption: A check-in that adapts to overwhelm with a smaller first step (illustrative).
One pass of the scheduler, from state to verified completion.
Under the hood: an Expo shell around a pure TypeScript engine.

decisions.title: The engine has no platform imports
decisions.desc: All scheduling and follow-up logic is pure TypeScript with no side effects, so it can serve Android, iOS, web and desktop — and be tested exhaustively.

decisions.title: Science over streak gimmicks
decisions.desc: Urgency and timing come from hyperbolic discounting, the procrastination equation and spaced repetition, not fixed reminder intervals.

decisions.title: Escalate, but with compassion
decisions.desc: Repeated ignores escalate to a full-screen check-in, while a guilt spiral triggers a compassion reset instead of more pressure.

decisions.title: Rewards you can't farm
decisions.desc: A completion verifier flags mass-completes and too-fast ticks, so XP reflects real follow-through.

roadmap: Launch the waitlist and pre-launch site.
iOS build and widgets from the same engine.
Metric-gated phases from the product brain before each expansion.

title: Carspace
summary: High-performance hybrid e-commerce marketplace for certified pre-owned vehicles — engineered with sub-100ms multi-facet inventory search, real-time Firestore database synchronization, and native-feeling offline PWA mobile capabilities.

features.title: Sub-100ms Faceted Search

features.desc: Live websocket-backed document updates that automatically reflect newly listed vehicles, sold reservations, and price changes without reloading.
features.title: Real-Time Firestore Inventory Sync

features.desc: Installable to mobile home screens with service worker offline caching, responsive touch gestures, and native app appearance.
features.title: Zero-Install PWA Mobile Parity

features.desc: Streamlined in-app direct inquiry pipeline connecting verified buyers to dealership representatives with one-tap WhatsApp and call actions.
features.title: Dealership & Buyer Inquiry Flow

highlights: High-speed multi-faceted vehicle filtering with sub-100ms response time
Real-time cloud database architecture powered by Firebase Firestore
Installable Progressive Web App with offline caching and native mobile UI
